sources.title: Learning to Use Imagination: Progress-Conditioned Future Utilization for World Action Models

sectionsRead: Section 4: Method, all subsections and Equations (6)–(36)
Section 5: Experiments, all subsections and Tables 1–15
Appendix 1: Detailed Experimental Setup, all subsections
omissions: Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.

The extraction-only figure gap was addressed by inspecting all 13 original figures and all 15 tables in the PDF. All 11 supplied text chunks were read individually, including references and appendices.

Identity/version scope: the title and all seven authors match the supplied catalog. The inspected artifact is arXiv:2609.06578v1, dated 6 September 2026. No other revision was supplied or compared. The IEEE TPAMI running header does not establish publication acceptance.
Separate code, project-page contents, videos and other supplements were not inspected; no experiment was reproduced.

synopsis: ProWAM learns execution progress from recent action–observation feedback and recurrent memory, then uses that state to redistribute imagined-future attention inside a joint video–action policy. Its strongest evidence combines executed manipulation results with ablations separating progress estimation from future utilization.

problem.text: Imagined futures have different utility during approach, contact and placement. ProWAM asks how action generation should adapt their influence as execution advances. Its motivating diagnostic compares failure-stage distributions and horizon-group perturbations; the former alone cannot establish absolute stage failure risk.

contributions.text: SS-DTPE learns latent progress slots using short-term feedback, Mamba memory, instruction-prefix alignment and temporal structure.
HPIM converts progress into a global gate and token-specific relevance inside action-to-future attention.
The authors report gains across five simulation benchmarks and two real robots; ablations support both progress representation and modulation.

inputs: Current visual observation and language instruction
Previously executed action and recurrent progress state
outputs: A low-level action chunk for receding-horizon execution
Jointly modeled future visual latents and updated progress tokens

steps.name: Extract execution feedback
steps.detail: Encode the observation and previous action. Language-conditioned FiLM modulates encoded visual tokens; bidirectional cross-attention links the executed command with its observed outcome. Fuse these streams into current evidence.

steps.name: Update progress memory
steps.detail: A selective Mamba recurrence filters previous progress before Progress Attention queries current evidence. The result is latent progress slots, not predefined phase labels or an externally supplied completion percentage.

steps.name: Estimate future relevance
steps.detail: The gate uses observation, instruction, progress and its change. Future-token queries attend to progress keys/values, undergo self-attention and receive mean-one relevance weights. This query direction agrees with Figure 3 and Equation (26).

steps.name: Modulate joint generation
steps.detail: Combine the gate and relevance with a middle-emphasized layer schedule. Add a log-bias only to action-query/future-key logits, normalizing across all valid keys. Video and action experts communicate through shared MoT attention; an action head predicts commands.

training.text: First train SS-DTPE on successful demonstrations: Gaussian instruction-prefix targets follow normalized time, an order penalty discourages backward semantic progress, and contrastive learning organizes temporal neighbors. Freeze SS-DTPE, then train WAM and HPIM with action/video rectified-flow losses and gate supervision.

The gate uses automatic weak labels. Gripper transitions and task-dependent height/motion cues identify contact windows, expanded by 20 frames on either side. Contact targets are zero, others one; unreliable labels are masked. Local relevance has no token-level labels.

Wan2.2-5B components combine with a 1B action expert, 32-action chunks, nine video frames and eight progress tokens. Stage 1 runs five epochs on four H100 GPUs, batch four per GPU; stage 2 runs ten epochs on eight H100s, batch sixteen per GPU. Both use AdamW, learning rate 0.0001, weight decay 0.01, cosine scheduling and clipping at 1.0.

inference.text: Reset memory at episode start, using a start-action token initially. At each replan, update progress from actual observation/action feedback, condition HPIM, generate and execute an action chunk. Figure 3 includes training future observations; deployment does not receive ground-truth future frames. Exact denoising steps and the executed chunk prefix are unspecified.

equations.explanation: Equation (6): progress tokens use observation O_t, preceding executed action a_{t-1}, instruction L and previous progress tokens.

Equations (28), (30), (32): F counts future tokens; rho is a relevance logit; omega is mean-one relevance; d is the gate; eta is the layer coefficient; beta modulates attention logits C. Indices t,l,i,f denote time, layer, action token and future token; epsilon stabilizes the logarithm.
Equations (23), (36): semantic alignment, order consistency and temporal contrast organize progress; action/video generation and gate supervision train stage 2. The lambdas weight the named losses.

results.setting: Four suites, 40 tasks, 50 demonstrations per task and 2,000 evaluation trials.
results.interpretation: Best reported average, but LingBot-VA scores higher on Long (98.5%). No uncertainty intervals are supplied.

results.setting: Clean/randomized evaluation, 100 trials per task; mixture of 2,500 clean and 25,000 randomized demonstrations.
results.interpretation: Reported average gain is 0.9 percentage points; embodied pretraining differs between these methods.

results.metric: SR (%), IS and PS (reported percentage scale)
results.interpretation: Improves complete success and intermediate progress; Fast-WAM SR gain is 10.0 percentage points.

results.setting: Eight task families, 30 variations, 100 episodes per task–variation pair.
results.interpretation: Absolute gains are 0.062 SR and 0.090 TP; TP concerns partial advancement.

results.setting: Five tasks; 250 demonstrations and 100 evaluations per task, 128×128 observations.
results.interpretation: A 6.4-point average gain, with substantial task variation rather than universal dominance.

results.setting: Eight tasks per platform, 150–200 demonstrations per task and 50 evaluation rollouts; average final cumulative stage completion.
results.value: Galaxea R1 Lite: 72; AgileX Cobot Magic: 71.
results.interpretation: Executed robot-task gains of 16 and 14 percentage points; these are not generated-video quality scores.

results.setting: Four tasks per platform with lighting, scene/object variation; 50 trials per task.
results.interpretation: Gains concern specified variations; they do not establish cross-robot transfer.

results.setting: Galaxea long-horizon tasks; controlled variants in Tables 8 and 11.
results.comparison: Neither module: 56; SS-DTPE alone: 66; stateless HPIM: 62. Fixing the gate to one: 58; uniform local relevance: 62.
results.interpretation: Both modules and modulation levels contribute. Single-module variants change the progress interface, limiting a pure factorial interpretation.

limitations.text: The authors identify structured tabletop tasks and limited cross-embodiment evaluation as boundaries; each robot retains its own training and action configuration.

Algebraically, mean modulation equals the layer coefficient because relevance averages one. A low gate interpolates toward uniform weighting; it does not turn future attention off or guarantee reduced total future-attention mass. This is narrower than the prose description of overall reliance.
Tables lack confidence intervals and training-seed dispersion. Time-based prefix targets and monotonicity also leave recovery, repeated subtasks and reordered instructions insufficiently tested.

reproduction.text: Reproduction needs pretrained video components, synchronized robot demonstrations with reliable proprioceptive traces, and benchmark success implementations. Appendix metrics defer IS/PS and TP semantics to official benchmarks.

Resolve omitted Gaussian width, temporal sampling, weak-label height/motion and segment/gap thresholds, denoising configuration and execution cadence. No latency or GPU-hour budget is supplied. Proposed comparisons should hold backbone, training budget and rollout protocol fixed.

reasoning.text: The catalog is unassigned, so there is no substantive recorded quadrant to confirm. Architecture evidence supports joint future/action prediction through shared MoT attention, with modality-specific experts and a separately trained frozen progress encoder. The core is a joint generator, not an inverse-dynamics decoder; calling the whole pipeline One Model requires a definition accommodating the auxiliary encoder.

discussionQuestions: Does learned progress remain useful when a task requires undoing an earlier step or instruction order differs from execution order?
Does the gate improve control by selecting future tokens, changing total attention mass, or both?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, byline, author footnote and arXiv margin
evidence.detail: The title and seven authors match the catalog. The artifact identifies arXiv:2609.06578v1 [cs.CV], 6 September 2026; three institutions are named.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 3.2 and Figure 2
evidence.detail: Five Galaxea tasks use 100 trials each. Failure distributions compare action-only and joint WAM variants; near/mid/long future-group perturbations produce stage-dependent completion drops.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–6, Section 3.1, Equations (1)–(11), Figure 3
evidence.detail: A joint generative process combines modality-specific video/action experts through shared MoT attention. Progress conditions modulation before the action head.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 4.2, Equations (12)–(17), Figure 3
evidence.detail: FiLM and bidirectional action–observation attention form current evidence. Mamba filters prior progress, which queries current evidence through Progress Attention.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section 4.2, Equations (18)–(23), Figure 4
evidence.detail: Gaussian prefix targets use normalized demonstration time, with monotonic-order and temporal-contrastive objectives. Gaussian width and contrastive sampling details are not numerically specified.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 8–9, Section 4.3, Equations (24)–(34)
evidence.detail: The gate consumes observation, instruction, progress and progress change. Future queries attend to progress keys/values; mean-one relevance combines with gate and layer schedule. Only action-to-future logits receive log-bias; normalization includes all valid keys.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 9–10, Section 4.4
evidence.detail: Train SS-DTPE independently, then freeze it for WAM/HPIM training. At deployment reset memory, initialize with a start-action token, and update progress for receding-horizon action chunks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Equation (35); pp. 21–22, Appendix Section 1.4, Equations (41)–(43)
evidence.detail: Gripper, task-dependent height and optional motion cues define anchors, merged across arms and expanded by 20 frames before/after. Contact targets are zero, other targets one; unreliable labels are masked. Segment/gap refinement thresholds are unspecified.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Section 5.1, Model Details and Training Details
evidence.detail: Wan2.2-5B and a 1B action expert use horizon 32, nine frames and eight progress tokens. Training uses 5 epochs on 4 H100s then 10 epochs on 8 H100s, AdamW and stated hyperparameters; inference solver steps and latency are not given.

evidence.location: PDF p. 19, Appendix Section 1.1
evidence.detail: LIBERO: 40 tasks, 2,000 trials. RoboTwin: 2,500 clean plus 25,000 randomized demonstrations. VLABench: ten tasks, 50 episodes each. RoboEval: 100 episodes per task–variation pair. Mikasa: 250 demonstrations and 100 evaluations per task.

evidence.location: PDF p. 21, Appendix Section 1.3, Equations (37)–(40)
evidence.detail: SR measures complete success; averages are task/suite means. IS/PS defer to benchmark definitions. Later cumulative real-world stages require all preceding stages to succeed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Table 1, ProWAM, Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA rows
evidence.detail: ProWAM Spatial/Object/Goal/Long is 99.6/100.0/98.8/97.8%, average 99.1%; Fast-WAM averages 97.6%; LingBot-VA averages 98.5% and scores 98.5% on Long.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Table 2, ProWAM and FlowWAM rows
evidence.detail: ProWAM Clean/Randomized/Avg. is 93.9/92.8/93.4%, without embodied pretraining; FlowWAM is 92.9/92.1/92.5%, with embodied pretraining.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Table 3 and asterisk definition; p. 12, VLABench discussion
evidence.detail: SR/IS/PS: ProWAM 68.4/85.4/81.2; author-reproduced Fast-WAM 58.4/81.2/74.5; pi0.5 65.4/80.4/77.8.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Table 4 and RoboEval discussion
evidence.detail: Across eight tasks and 30 variations, ProWAM SR/TP is 0.375/0.494 versus author-reproduced Fast-WAM 0.313/0.404.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Table 5
evidence.detail: ProWAM scores 94/68/48/24/20% on SGT/IM/RC3/RC5/RC9, average 50.8%; MemoryVLA++ averages 44.4%. ProWAM does not win every task.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Section 5.2; pp. 19–21, Appendix Section 1.2
evidence.detail: Real tasks use 150–200 demonstrations and 50 evaluation rollouts. Eight long-horizon and four robustness tasks run on Galaxea R1 Lite and AgileX Cobot Magic, with randomized positions and stated variations.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Tables 6–7, Avg. columns and dagger definitions
evidence.detail: Long-horizon full-task success: Galaxea/AgileX 72/71% versus Fast-WAM 56/57%; robustness 69/68% versus 58/57%. Daggered baselines were author-reproduced under the same training/deployment settings.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Section 5.5 setup; p. 13, Table 8 and component-ablation discussion
evidence.detail: Galaxea Long./Gen.: 56/58 without either module, 66/65 for directly fused SS-DTPE, 62/64 for stateless-context HPIM, 72/69 for the full model.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 13–14, Tables 9–10 and accompanying discussion
evidence.detail: Mamba outperforms listed no-aggregator, LSTM and Transformer variants. Galaxea Long.: semantic alignment alone 59%, with order consistency 67%, with temporal structure 72%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14, Tables 11–14 and Sections 5.5–5.6
evidence.detail: Table 11 fixes d=1 without Inter., uses uniform relevance without Intra., and compares layer schedules. Galaxea Long.: 58/62/72% for these variants/full model; uniform schedule 70%. Time-Only Long./Gen. is 56/59% versus SS-DTPE 72/69%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Table 15
evidence.detail: Galaxea Long./Gen.: 59/61% without gate supervision, 72/69% with it; 20% label perturbation yields 68/66%. No seed variance or confidence intervals are shown.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Section 5.6 relevance-analysis paragraph; p. 16, Figure 10
evidence.detail: Normalize relevance to mass one, pool by future frame, and rank across frames/views/positions. LIBERO-Spatial top-20% mass is 93.0/44.7/89.5% for approach/lift/transport, with frame splits 95:5/49:51/78:22.

evidence.location: PDF p. 23, Appendix Section 3
evidence.detail: Evaluation is relatively structured tabletop manipulation. Large-scale cross-embodiment transfer is outside scope; training, observations and action representations remain platform-specific.
